newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ pre-election rate cut seen as too risky.
newsitem.headline: NZ pre-election rate cut seen as too risky.

text.p: Economists say the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will not explicitly ease monetary policy a month before a general election, but may not object if the market starts to nudge rates lower.
The bank, still fighting to bring underlying inflation back within its 0-2 percent target band from 2.3 percent in June, will issue its half-yearly economic projections on Friday.
Economists say that with inflation set to fall next year and New Zealand interest rates among the world's highest in real terms, an eventual easing is largely a matter of timing.
"The problem is, between now and when those interest rates decline is the October 12 election," said Adrian Orr, Chief Economist at National Bank of New Zealand Ltd.
"I think the Reserve Bank will be very nervous to signal a rate easing right now, when God knows what will be happening to the exchange rate over the next couple of months."

The October election is a leap into the unknown, New Zealand's first under proportional representation. The conservative government leads in opinion polls, but three left-of-centre parties look set to gain more than half the vote and could oust it if they can set aside their differences.
A left-wing government would raise spending, limiting the central bank's scope to cut interest rates because of the risk of reigniting inflation. It could also amend the bank's inflation target.
Other unknowns include the impact on growth and inflation of tax cuts which took effect on July 1, the first round of a $3.1 billion (US$2.15 billion) two-year package.
"There's all those imponderables which I think, at the end of the day, tip the balance and say well, you can't ease, it's too risky," said SBC Warburg economist Robin Clements.
On the other hand, monetary conditions have actually firmed well beyond what the RBNZ signalled as necessary in its last big set-piece statement in June.
The Trade-Weighted Index, which measures the New Zealand dollar against a basket of other currencies, has firmed to around 65.6 from the 64.0 assumed by the central bank.

"That leaves a lot of room for the market itself to take rates lower, even without an official endorsement from the RB," Orr said. Clements agreed the bank "wouldn't get too upset if conditions eased a little bit".
Ten economists polled by Reuters were unanimous the bank would signal no explicit easing on Friday.

Merchant bank Bancorp Treasury Services sees a market-led easing in October, with the Reserve Bank sanctioning the move by not commenting. Seven economists picked an easing in November or December, while two believe it won't happen until next year.
On average, the economists predicted GDP growth of just under 1.8 percent between the March quarter of 1996 and the March quarter of 1997, doubling to 3.6 the following year.
That compares with RBNZ forecasts in June of two to 2.5 percent for both years.
The Treasury, in a Pre-Election Economic and Fiscal Update on Thursday, is also expected to revise its near-term growth predictions downwards.
At the time of the government budget last May, Treasury was forecasting annual average growth of 2.6 percent and four percent respectively for the 1996-97 and 1997-98 March years.
Finance Minister Bill Birch last month acknowledged growth had slowed somewhat but said this was no cause for concern.
